newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to meet with Big Three auto chiefs in May.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to meet with Big Three auto chiefs in May.

text.p: President Clinton is tentatively scheduled to meet with the chairmen of Detroit's Big Three automakers in mid-May to discuss broad-ranging industry issues, a Ford Motor Co. spokesman said Friday.

Al Chambers, Ford's director of corporate public affairs, said the meeting is intended to replace an April 3 gathering canceled by Clinton, which was scheduled to include Ford Chairman Alex Trotman, General Motors Corp. GM.N Chairman John Smith, Chrysler Corp. C.N Chairman Robert Eaton and United Auto Workers President Stephen Yokich.
Chambers declined to disclose the exact date of the rescheduled meeting.
The Big Three chiefs earlier this week met briefly with Vice President Al Gore during his stay in Detroit, but the subject of the meeting was empowerment zones and new investments in Detroit.
Chambers and Chrysler spokesman Chris Preuss said the automakers want to discuss a broad range of issues with Clinton, but do not intend to make any demands.
Discussion will include the dollar's strength against the Japenese yen, which has helped Japanese automakers gain U.S. market share, but that will not be the main topic of discussion.
"Some people think this is a complaining thing. It's not. It's a good dialogue," Chambers said.

Preuss, who did not confirm plans for the mid-May meeting, said automakers have been trying to set up a gathering similar to one held in Little Rock, Ark., in late 1992 just before Clinton took office for his first term.
"We're making known our views on various issues affecting the industry," Preuss said. "Obviously dollar-yen is part of that."

Other topics of discussion would include the industry's concerns about possible future increases in the government's Coporate Average Fuel Economy standards. The Big Three have opposed increases in the required fleet average of 27.5 miles per gallon for cars and 20.5 miles per gallon for trucks.
Other topics would include international negotiations to reduce global warming and safety regulations, including proposed new rules to make air bags safer.
